title: Map of the British Isles: how far did the ice reach?
subject: Geography
source: Written for geography/y7 lesson 9 (Map of the British Isles with the ice limit (portal printable))
intro: Lesson 9. Shade the area covered by ice at the peak of the last glacial period, using the map on the slides, and label the ice limit.

blocks.caption: Outline from Natural Earth (public domain); modern coastlines and borders.

questions.a: Snow builds up, is squashed into firn and then ice, which flows downhill under gravity
questions.model: Start: snow builds up each winter. Next: the weight squashes it into ice. Then: gravity makes it flow downhill. So a glacier forms.

questions.q: About what fraction of land is covered by ice today?
Why was sea level lower 20,000 years ago?
questions.a: So much water was locked up in ice on land

questions.q: Core: On a map of the British Isles, shade the ice cover 20,000 years ago and mark your home. Write two sentences on what your area was like.
questions.a: Ice over most of Scotland, Wales, northern England and Ireland; south of that, cold tundra; sentences match the pupil's location
questions.model: Teacher shows it first: shade from northern Scotland down to roughly the Bristol Channel and the Midlands, then mark London outside the ice: 'London was not under ice but was frozen tundra.'

questions.q: Extend: Compare the size of glaciers 20,000 years ago with today.
questions.a: Far more of the land, including much of Britain, was covered then; today about 10% of land

questions.q: Stretch: Explain why Britain was joined to Europe then.
questions.a: Water was stored as ice, so sea level fell and the seabed between Britain and Europe was dry land

questions.q: Big question: what would your home town have looked like 20,000 years ago?
questions.a: Depending on location: under thick ice in the north and west, or cold, treeless tundra in the south
